defects.defect: Length breaches the 5-page cap on Part 1. The method content alone runs to roughly 3,900 words (approach logic ~390, evidence engine ~185, stakeholder engagement ~200, twelve week-rows with four fields each ~1,150, eight method steps ~1,200, seven risk/mitigation pairs ~820). At normal proposal density that is 6-8 pages for methodology alone. But RFP Part 1 must ALSO hold, inside the same 5 pages: 'An understanding of the consultancy requirements', 'Detailed reference list indicating the scope and magnitude of similar assignments' and 'Relevant services undertaken in the past five (5) years'. Only CVs are permitted in an annex (Part 2). As drafted, Part 1 is non-responsive on format before a single word is scored.
defects.fix: Cut the method narrative to roughly 1,400-1,600 words so Part 1 totals under 5 pages. Compress the 12-week table to a single Gantt-style strip (week / activity / deliverable / CI input) and move the four-field week detail, the eight method steps' 'why' column and the full risk register into annexes. Confirm with CI in a clarification question whether annexes are unlimited. Keep in the body only: understanding of the ToR, the headline approach logic, the week strip, the nine-heading and nine-criterion frames, the reference list and the past-five-years services.

defects.defect: Communities and visitors are excluded from the appetite test, though CI names them as two of the six perspectives every model must be elaborated against. Week 10 session one is 'CI and core Keystone partners'; week 11 session two is 'park authorities, a national tourism board, a co-management partner and private sector trade'; and the risk-4 minimum-coverage rule requires only 'one national government or tourism board, one park authority, one co-management partner and one private sector voice'. No community representative and no visitor or source-market voice appears anywhere in the interview list, the session invite lists or the coverage rule. For a conservation client whose design aims require models to be 'sensitive, conservation-led, evidence-based and culturally appropriate', this is the first thing an evaluator will notice.
defects.fix: Add community and visitor/demand-side representation explicitly. For communities: name a community conservancy or community trust voice distinct from the association secretariats (NRT, NACSO and MMWCA are association proxies, not community voices), and add 'at least one community representative' to the minimum-coverage rule. For visitors: substitute a source-market trade voice (inbound tour operator or DMC) plus CI's own visitation data. Restate the minimum-coverage rule as covering all six CI lenses.

defects.defect: The 'geography-agnostic' mitigation cuts directly against a scored RFP requirement. Risk 2's mitigation states 'The option architecture is built geography-agnostic; geography enters only in the rollout sequencing annex.' But RFP 5.2 requires the bidder to 'Evaluate and assess the model concepts for suitability in the case of protected areas across Africa (especially the CI priority areas)', and evaluation criterion 2.4 awards 10 of 70 technical points for 'Geographical Reach & Familiarity'. Relegating geography to an annex is the opposite of what is scored, and states it in writing.
defects.fix: Reframe the mitigation: the option architecture is built against a documented assumption set of representative area archetypes (transfrontier, single-country emerging, conservancy-adjacent, coastal/marine) drawn from the benchmark scan, and is re-tested against CI's actual fifteen areas at the week six screening gate. Suitability assessment against CI priority areas stays in the body of the report, not an annex. Separately, build a visible geographical-reach section elsewhere in Part 1 to answer criterion 2.4.

defects.defect: The week six screening gate drops nothing. Week 6 and method step 5 both state that four candidate configurations are built and then 'screened with CI to carry three plus one reserve'. Three carried plus one reserve is four. Yet the week 6 output is a 'screening decision log recording what was dropped and why' and method step 5 claims 'the screening log gives the final report a defensible account of what was dropped'. Nothing is dropped, so the log is empty and the gate is decorative. It also leaves ambiguity on whether the reserve is elaborated under the nine headings in weeks 7-8 ('each carried option'), which is the difference between three and four full elaborations of CI's nine headings and the ten-year model.
defects.fix: Build five or six configurations in week 6 and screen to three plus one reserve, so the log has real content. State explicitly that the three carried options receive the full nine-heading elaboration and the ten-year model, and that the reserve is held as a one-page configuration note re-openable at the week nine sensitivity test. That also protects the RFP's 'at least three' floor with margin.

defects.defect: The nine-column matrix is presented as CI's design aims, which it is not. The approach logic states 'CI's design aims become the nine-column scoring matrix, already built and populated for 31 cases' and the evidence engine says benchmarks are 'rated against nine criteria drawn from CI's design aims'. EY's own scan says the opposite in Section 4: 'CI's terms of reference list seven aims for any model. We rated each benchmark against six of them, plus two conditions from Activity Two (operating across jurisdictions and working for sites of wide-ranging capacity) and a flag for African evidence.' So two of the nine columns are EY-added conditions and one ('African evidence') is a research-maturity flag with no meaning when applied to score EY's own designed options. Further, CI's sixth aim is 'mechanisms that support multi-stakeholder brand management, including reconciling alignment with national destination brands' and the matrix reduces it to 'National brand fit', dropping the multi-stakeholder brand management half. An evaluator holding the ToR beside the matrix sees the mismatch.
defects.fix: Describe the frame accurately: 'six of CI's seven design aims, plus two delivery conditions drawn from Activity Two (cross-jurisdiction operation, wide-ranging site capacity), with the seventh aim - filling gaps rather than duplicating effort - tested separately by the crowding map.' Split 'National brand fit' into two columns, 'multi-stakeholder brand management' and 'national destination brand alignment', so all of aim six is scored. For option scoring, replace 'African evidence' with 'strength of precedent' or drop it to eight columns.

defects.defect: Only nine of the thirteen organisations the plan depends on receive a week-one interview request, which breaks the proposal's own central argument. Week 1 and method step 1 commit to issuing requests to 'nine named secretariats and platforms', and placeholder 4 confirms those nine are Boundless Southern Africa, Africa's Eden Tourism, KAZA Secretariat, NRT, NACSO, MMWCA, The Long Run, Preferred Hotel Group and SLH. But the stakeholder engagement section names four more: Slovenia Green, Tourism Australia (Signature Experiences), SANParks and EUROPARC. Slovenia Green and Signature Experiences of Australia are Tier 1 case studies in the scan and are scheduled for deep-dive in week 4 (block B). The proposal's own load-bearing claim is that 'a cold approach to a regional secretariat takes three to four weeks to land' - so requesting them after week one guarantees they miss the week four deep-dive and the week five Deliverable 2.
defects.fix: Issue all thirteen requests in week one and say so. Change week 1 to 'Issue interview requests to thirteen named secretariats, boards and platforms' and update method step 1 and placeholder 4 to the same thirteen, marking which relationships CI is asked to broker and which EY approaches cold.

defects.defect: The committed interview count is smaller than the plan's own named target list. Stakeholder engagement states 'We target sixteen interviews with twelve as the floor'. The plan then names thirteen organisations in that section, plus in week 8 'lodges, operators, a national tourism board and the hosting platforms', plus in week 8 CI involvement 'two or three park authorities and one co-management partner'. That is roughly twenty distinct interviews implied. At the stated floor of twelve, the programme cannot even cover the thirteen named organisations, let alone the payer-side and park-authority interviews the appetite test depends on.
defects.fix: Either raise the target to twenty with a floor of sixteen and cost it against the effort table, or reduce the named list to match. If the count is budget-constrained, tier it explicitly: thirteen core organisational interviews as the committed floor, plus up to seven appetite interviews contingent on CI-brokered introductions. Do not publish a floor the named plan already exceeds.

defects.defect: There is no instrument anywhere in the method for demand-side or segment evidence, yet 'Support multi segment stratification and destination appeal' is one of CI's seven design aims and 'Segments and appeal' is a scored column in the evaluation matrix. Every evidence source in the plan is supply-side: secretariats, associations, certification bodies, hotel platforms and tourism boards. No source-market data, no visitation or booking data, no operator demand view, no consumer or trade segmentation work. Placeholder 10 asks CI for any market demand or visitation data it holds, which is a request, not a method. If CI holds nothing, the plan has no way to score its own 'segments and appeal' column above a guess.
defects.fix: Add a named demand-side step in week 4: a trade and demand read drawing on published inbound arrivals and source-market data for the priority countries, operator product listings showing which emerging areas already appear in itineraries, plus two inbound operator or DMC interviews. Make the fallback explicit if CI holds no data, rather than leaving the column unsupported.

defects.defect: Western Africa is absent from the entire evidence base and interview programme. The RFP states the fifteen areas 'are spread across Southern, Eastern and Western Africa'. Every African benchmark in the scan and every African interview target in the plan is Southern or Eastern African: Boundless Southern Africa (SADC), Africa's Eden Tourism (eight SADC-region countries), KAZA (five countries), NRT, NACSO, MMWCA, SANParks, Visit Rwanda, Fair Trade Tourism (Southern and Eastern). With 10 of 70 technical points on geographical reach and familiarity, a West African evaluator sees a Southern African firm proposing a Southern African evidence base. The plan also does not flag that the RFP contradicts itself - 'prioritized 15 emerging protected areas in Southern and Eastern Africa' in one sentence, 'spread across Southern, Eastern and Western Africa' in the next.
defects.fix: Add a clarification question asking CI to resolve the Southern/Eastern versus Southern/Eastern/Western contradiction and to confirm whether any of the fifteen areas sit in West or Central Africa. Add at least one West or Central African reference point to the deep-dive set or the light-touch checks and name it. Add a placeholder for EY West Africa capability if the answer is yes.

defects.defect: 'We said so in writing before being asked' (approach logic, closing line) claims a prior written disclosure to CI that did not happen. The statement being referred to is in EY's internal working draft, dated 19 September 2026 and headed 'EY bid team working draft 2', which CI has never seen - and placeholder 8 itself concedes that whether the scan may even be cited or shared is unconfirmed. In a proposal, that sentence reads as 'we told you this before you asked us', which is a claim about the client relationship that cannot be substantiated. It is the one line in the analysis that asserts something not in evidence.
defects.fix: Replace with a factual formulation that does not claim prior disclosure, for example: 'This scoping anchor was fixed in our own research before this proposal was written, not reverse-engineered from the budget line.' Resolve placeholder 8 first, since the sentence is only usable at all if the scan can be cited.

defects.defect: Week 2 commits the unverified rating matrix into a client deliverable, contradicting the plan's own control and its own placeholder. The week 2 output is 'Deliverable 1: Inception Report, carrying the 31-benchmark long-list, the archetype map and the rating matrix as Annex A.' But the scan states its figures 'have not yet been verified with the organisations concerned' and its ratings are 'team judgement on the desk evidence'; verification does not happen until weeks 3-4 under method step 2; and placeholder 8 says it is unconfirmed whether the scan may be cited at all, shared with CI, or attached as an annex. The plan therefore commits in writing to an annex it has not been cleared to release, containing figures its own method says must be graded before they carry weight.
defects.fix: Make the Annex A commitment conditional on resolving placeholder 8, and if released, carry a stated status line on it: 'long-list as at [date], published figures not yet verified with the organisations concerned; ratings are team judgement and will move as deep-dives land.' Better: commit only the archetype map and long-list in week 2, and release the rating matrix with Deliverable 2 in week 5 once graded.

defects.defect: 'seven tested POV signals' (evidence engine) is wrong. The scan's Section 6 carries eight early signals: aggregation saves most in the back office; in Africa the aggregation layer often already exists; Africa's best-known lodges are already curated; brands last when someone pays for what they deliver; credibility comes from standards with consequences; national brands must be partners not rivals; consumer memberships are real money but cyclical and slow to build; outside money comes with strings. This is a number an EY reviewer or a diligent evaluator checks against the annexed scan in seconds.
defects.fix: Change 'seven tested POV signals' to 'eight tested POV signals'.

defects.defect: 'the commercial terms nobody publishes have eleven weeks to surface rather than six' (evidence engine) uses two different endpoints. Eleven weeks of runway from a week one request implies an endpoint at week twelve. Six weeks of runway from the week four baseline the same paragraph invokes ('Interview requests go out in week one rather than week four') implies an endpoint at week ten. Measured consistently to week twelve the comparison is eleven versus eight; measured consistently to week ten it is nine versus six. Neither pairing produces eleven and six.
defects.fix: Pick one endpoint and state it. Measured to the week ten draft report, the honest comparison is 'nine weeks to surface rather than six'. Measured to the week twelve final, it is 'eleven weeks rather than eight'.

defects.defect: RFP 5.2 states 'Pre-requisites will also be important to consider' as an explicit requirement of Activity Two. The method never addresses pre-requisites. Nothing in the nine-heading elaboration (weeks 7-8), the option architecture (week 6) or the evaluation (week 9) covers what must be true before a given model can be stood up - legal standing, host agreements, data and IP arrangements, government consent, minimum member base, seed capital.
defects.fix: Add a pre-requisites line to the option canvas in week 7 and a pre-requisites column to the scoring workbook in week 9, covering legal vehicle and registration, host or platform agreement, government and tourism-board consent, minimum viable membership, seed funding and data/IP arrangements. Carry the pre-requisites of the preferred model into the Activity Three Terms of Reference.

defects.defect: The workplan front-loads effort into weeks 1-2 while the RFP caps the inception report at no more than 10% of the payment schedule. Weeks 1-2 carry the kick-off, the stakeholder and priority-area confirmation, the evaluation frame, the risk and assumption log, the interview request programme to nine (properly thirteen) organisations, the full inception report, and the start of Tier 1 desk verification on three benchmarks. That is materially more than a tenth of the twelve-week effort, but only a tenth of the fee can attach to Deliverable 1. The method analysis does not flag this interaction for the cost workstream.
defects.fix: Either move the Tier 1 desk verification start out of week 2 into week 3 so weeks 1-2 carry inception work only, or flag explicitly to the cost workstream that inception-phase effort exceeds the 10% payment tranche and must be recovered against Deliverable 2. Add this to the placeholder for the effort table.

defects.defect: The named substitute for SLH is already a primary target, so it provides no redundancy. Risk 1's mitigation reads 'Preferred Hotel Group where SLH declines' - but Preferred Hotel Group is already on the week-one request list in its own right (for Beyond Green), named in placeholder 4 as one of the nine. If the commercial hotel platforms decline as a class, which is the actual risk given that none of them publishes member fees, both the primary and the substitute fail together. The other two substitutes named (KWCA for MMWCA, Ecotourism Kenya and Botswana's ecotourism certification for Fair Trade Tourism) are sound and correctly drawn from the scan's Section 8.
defects.fix: Name a genuinely independent substitute for the hosted-collection question - for example Relais & Chateaux or National Geographic Unique Lodges, both already in the scan and both holding the same build-host-or-borrow evidence - and keep Preferred Hotel Group as a primary.

defects.defect: 'a cold approach to a regional secretariat takes three to four weeks to land' is asserted twice, in the approach logic and in method step 1, with no source and no basis. It is the single load-bearing claim of the whole 'Thirty-one to One' differentiator: the argument that starting interviews in week one rather than week four is decisive rests entirely on it. An evaluator who does not accept the figure loses the argument, and EY has offered nothing to make it stick.
defects.fix: Either ground it - 'in our experience of approaching regional secretariats and member associations, first substantive response typically takes three to four weeks' is honest and attributable to EY practice - or drop the number and make the structural argument instead: requests issued in week one leave the whole programme as contingency, requests issued in week four leave none.

defects.defect: Placeholder coverage stops short of three Part 1 and submission requirements the RFP names explicitly. There is no placeholder for: the 'Detailed reference list indicating the scope and magnitude of similar assignments' and 'Relevant services undertaken in the past five (5) years' required in Part 1 - note the RFP says five years here while scoring criterion 2.2 says three years with samples of work delivered, a discrepancy the bid must resolve; the 'at least three client references' required in Part 3; and the 'Signed Offeror Representation of Transparency, Integrity, Social Responsibility' listed as a submission completeness item. Placeholder 8 usefully asks whether the benchmark scan can serve as a sample of work, but no placeholder asks for the samples themselves.
defects.fix: Add placeholders: [[TO CONFIRM: EY reference list of similar assignments with scope and magnitude, covering both the past five years (Part 1 requirement) and the past three years with samples of work delivered (scoring criterion 2.2) - supplied by Michael Harris and EY Business Consulting]]; [[TO CONFIRM: three client references with named contacts and permission to approach - supplied by Michael Harris]]; [[TO CONFIRM: signed Offeror Representation of Transparency, Integrity, Social Responsibility - EY legal/compliance]]. Also raise a clarification question on the five-year versus three-year discrepancy.

defects.defect: Activity Two begins before CI's feedback on Activity One arrives. Week 6 builds four configurations and runs the screening session, while the week 5 and week 6 CI involvement entries both state that consolidated written comments on Deliverable 2 are due at end of week six. So the option set is constructed and screened on a situational analysis CI has not yet commented on. The schedule is defensible for the week twelve date but reads as processing CI's second deliverable as a formality.
defects.fix: Move the week six screening session to late in week six, after comments land, or bring the comment deadline forward to Wednesday of week six as is done at week eleven. Either way, state in the week six row that the screening session is run against CI's comments, not before them.

strengths: Integrity is clean. There is not one invented EY credential, client name, staff name, day rate, legal entity or reference anywhere in the analysis. Michael Harris appears only as the named supplier of placeheld inputs, which is what the brief authorises.

Placeholder 7 holds the hardest line correctly: rather than dress the method in a plausible-sounding EY framework name, it uses descriptive frame names (the nine-heading option canvas, the nine-criterion matrix, the three switches, the cost-to-serve and revenue-stack model) and asks explicitly whether a proprietary EY asset name should replace them. This is exactly the failure mode most bids fall into and it has been avoided deliberately and stated.

Placeholder 1 correctly identifies the RFP truncation, quotes the exact cut point ('largely desk-based with virtual'), and reasons properly about the consequence - that the missing Level of Effort text may specify days, team composition or virtual engagement requirements that change the workplan and the effort table. It routes it to a written clarification question before submission rather than assuming.

The source-grading control (method step 2) turns the scan's own honesty caveat into a method discipline. Three grades, every figure dated and graded in the report, and a hard rule that nothing below the top two grades drives the base case of the financial model. It directly answers the scan's stated weakness ('figures are as published... not yet verified with the organisations concerned') and it names the stale figures it is designed to catch.

Writing all thirteen deep-dives to CI's nine model-elaboration headings, so benchmark evidence drops straight into option design rather than being re-cut, is a genuinely tight structural move and is traceable line by line to RFP 5.1 and the nine elaboration bullets. The scan's own Section 7 recommends exactly this, so it is consistent with the head start EY actually holds.

The end-game schedule arithmetic is correct and protective. Deliverable 3 issued on day one of week ten rather than at the end, session two early in week eleven, consolidated comments due that Wednesday - which leaves Thursday and Friday of week eleven plus five days of week twelve, exactly the seven working days claimed. Routing late comments into the Activity Three next-steps register rather than reopening the report is a sound way to hold the week twelve date.

The benchmark facts drawn from the scan are accurate. ECST's fall from 164 areas to 91, Alpine Pearls from 24 villages to 18, LHW dropping its paid Leaders Club in 2021, NRT's 2016 fundraising, the eighteen years of Boundless Southern Africa, Africa's Eden Tourism domiciled in Botswana, the eight-plus-five split of thirteen deep-dives, the seven archetype names, the three cross-cutting switches, and the substitutes drawn from the scan's Section 8 - all check out against the source.

The risk register names exactly the right organisations for the evidence gaps. 'None of LHW, Relais et Chateaux, SLH, Preferred Hotel Group, National Geographic or The Long Run publishes member fees' and 'no published recognition or booking measures exist for Boundless Southern Africa or KAZA' map precisely onto gaps one and two in the scan's Section 8, and the mitigation - any figure not obtained shown as a stated range with its source class, never as fact - is the right commercial answer.

Placeholder 9 on French and Portuguese is a real, well-reasoned risk correctly grounded in the evidence: Angola, Mozambique and Madagascar genuinely recur across the benchmark set (Africa's Eden Tourism's eight countries, Fair Trade Tourism's certification footprint, KAZA's partner states), and translation plus a Lusophone or Francophone interviewer would have to be costed against a fixed US$40,000.

Agreeing the evaluation weights with CI before any score is entered, then publishing the two or three assumptions that would flip the result, is a credible integrity control that answers the 'pre-cooked recommendation' objection an evaluator will otherwise raise against a bidder who arrives with a benchmark scan already built.

defects.defect: The matrix has no row for submission logistics: no deadline, no submission method or address, no proposal validity period, no clarification-questions deadline, no named CI contact, no language/format requirement. Nor does it flag that the RFP pack we hold begins at "2. Procurement details" - Section 1, which in CI's template carries exactly these items, is simply not in our file. It also ignores the blank "Other:" row in the Section 4 completeness table. A compliance matrix that answers 74 content questions but never answers "when and how is this lodged" is not a control document for responsiveness; a late or wrongly-routed submission scores zero irrespective of every other row.
defects.fix: Add rows C-75 to C-79 covering: (a) [[TO CONFIRM: CI to supply the complete RFP including Section 1 and all submission instructions - our pack starts at Section 2]]; (b) submission deadline, date and time zone; (c) submission channel (email address or portal) and any file-size/naming convention; (d) proposal validity period EY will offer, noting CI states the cost proposal "serves as a basis of negotiation"; (e) the "Other:" line item in the Section 4 table. Make the deadline row the first row in the matrix and the first item in qa/open_items.md.

defects.defect: C-15 contradicts itself on the page cap and the contradiction propagates. Its whereMet and evidenceNeeded scope the 5 pages to "Part 1 body", and formatRules states "Technical Proposal Part 1 is capped at a maximum of 5 pages" - but its risk field instructs "Build to the strictest reading: 5 pages for the whole technical narrative excluding annexes." Those are mutually exclusive build instructions. The strict reading is also unbuildable: it would force Part 1's four bullets plus C-09 (staffing plan), C-11 (corporate capabilities), C-12 (project descriptions) and C-13 (three references) into the same 5 pages, contradicting the whereMet allocations in C-04 through C-13. The RFP text settles it - "A technical proposal, max 5 pages (excluding annexes)" appears once, at line 101, inside the right-hand cell of the Part 1 row only; Parts 2 and 3 have their own cells with their own separate guidance.
defects.fix: Delete the "strictest reading" sentence from C-15's risk field. Fix the cap as Part 1 only, and add a visible one-line assumption on the technical proposal cover page: "Part 1 is presented within the 5-page limit; Parts 2 and 3 and all annexes are presented separately, per the Part-by-Part structure of Section 4." Log a clarification question to CI in case they intend the cap to cover all three Parts.

defects.defect: C-14 and C-07 issue contradictory instructions that will collide at QA. C-14's evidenceNeeded forbids "no cost, rate, day-rate or fee figure anywhere in the technical PDF (including annexes, CVs, headers and footers)". C-07's evidenceNeeded requires, for every reference assignment, "contract value or level of effort (this is the 'magnitude' test)" - and that reference list lives in the technical PDF (Part 1 section 3 and Annex B). Contract values are fee figures. As written, satisfying C-07 breaches C-14, and satisfying C-14 strips the magnitude evidence the RFP explicitly demands in Part 1 bullet 3. Separately, C-14 states as a format rule something the RFP does not say: the RFP requires separate PDFs and says only technically qualified bidders' financials are opened; it nowhere prohibits cost figures in the technical document.
defects.fix: Rewrite C-14's prohibition to bite only on EY's pricing for THIS assignment: no day rate, fee, line item, total or discount relating to RFP 0032026 may appear in the technical PDF. Explicitly permit historical contract values and LOE for past assignments in Part 1 section 3 and Annex B, since the RFP requires them. Re-label C-14's two-envelope claim as EY's inference rather than an RFP rule, and write the QA sweep against the corrected wording.

defects.defect: The RFP's evaluation table runs 1.1, 1.2, 2.1, 2.2, 2.4, 3.1 - there is no 2.3. The matrix transcribes all six criteria faithfully (C-67 to C-72) but never registers that a sub-criterion number is missing from the issued table. This matters because the document is demonstrably incomplete elsewhere (it terminates mid-sentence at "largely desk-based with virtual"), so a dropped row in the evaluation table is a live possibility rather than a typo. If CI's master contains a 2.3 that our screenshot lost, EY would be leaving an entire scored criterion unanswered while believing the matrix is complete.
defects.fix: Add a row: "Evaluation table numbering skips 2.3. [[TO CONFIRM: CI to confirm whether sub-criterion 2.3 exists and, if so, its wording and weighting - the issued table omits it and the six listed weights already total 70]]." Include it in the clarification questions sent to CI before the deadline, and hold it as an open item until answered.

defects.defect: The RFP ends mid-sentence - "This assignment is expected to be largely desk-based with virtual" - and no row in the matrix requires EY to obtain the missing text. C-21 mentions the truncation only in passing, as something EY's own LOE working "mitigates". It does not mitigate it. The severed sentence sits in "Level of Effort and Cost of Services", the section most likely to state CI's expected number of consultant days, the expected virtual engagement arrangements, and possibly the basis on which the 30-mark financial score is judged. Building a fixed-price bid against a truncated pricing section, under a rule that costs cannot be revised after submission (C-17), is an uncontrolled commercial exposure.
defects.fix: Add a row: "[[TO CONFIRM: CI to supply the complete 'Level of Effort and Cost of Services' section - our copy terminates mid-sentence after 'largely desk-based with virtual'. Specifically needed: any stated expected level of effort in days, any stated expectation on virtual engagement/interviews, and any further cost-proposal instructions.]]" Rate it High and make it a week-1 chase alongside C-03.

defects.defect: C-22 asserts as established fact that this is "a cross-border service to a US-registered non-profit" and builds the whole tax row on it, including the South African zero-rating analysis. Nothing in the RFP identifies CI's contracting entity or its jurisdiction. Conservation International operates through regional and country entities, and an RFP for Africa-based work may well be contracted from a CI Africa entity - in which case the export-of-services zero-rating conclusion flips and the withholding-tax position changes. C-22's own placeholder asks EY to confirm the EY entity but not the CI counterparty, so the assumption never gets tested. At a US$40,000 ceiling with no post-submission revision permitted, a wrong VAT assumption is a direct hit to margin or a loss on price.
defects.fix: Strip the "US-registered non-profit" assertion from C-22's evidenceNeeded. Add to the existing placeholder: "[[TO CONFIRM: CI to confirm the contracting legal entity and its country of registration for this engagement, and whether it holds a tax exemption or VAT status relevant to a South African supplier]]". State in the cost proposal's tax section the entity assumption actually used, so any error is visible and attributable rather than buried.

defects.defect: C-70 proposes that "where none can be released, EY's own CI benchmark research draft may be offered as a demonstrable sample of current work" against criterion 2.2. Criterion 2.2 asks for "relevant services provided in the last three years with samples of work delivered" - work delivered to clients. A bid-preparation working draft produced for this very pursuit is not a service provided to a client and is not work delivered. Offering it as one against a 15-mark criterion signals to an evaluator that EY has no releasable client work, which is worse than a thin but honest entry. The draft also carries its own caveat - "All figures are as published by the sources below... They have not yet been verified with the organisations concerned" - so submitting it as a quality exemplar exposes unverified figures to scrutiny.
defects.fix: Remove the benchmark draft from C-70 as a criterion 2.2 response. Keep the placeholder for genuine cleared client samples and rate the row High until it closes. If EY wants the head start visible, position an extract of the scan separately in Part 1 as evidence of readiness and method, clearly labelled as bid-stage work produced at EY's own cost, and remove or verify any figure that is source-published but unconfirmed.

defects.defect: The matrix does not distinguish between placeholders EY can close before submission and placeholders only CI can close, yet the QA gate requires zero placeholders in the released PDFs. C-40's placeholder asks CI for the list of 15 priority areas; C-43's asks CI for its ToR template. Neither is realistically answerable pre-award - EY's own research draft says the 15 areas should be requested "at inception". So these are inception-stage data requests wearing the same [[TO CONFIRM]] clothing as genuine pre-submission blockers like C-03 (CI's representation template, which genuinely must clear before lodgement) and C-19 (EY day rates). Treated as blockers they stall the bid; left in place they breach the no-placeholder rule.
defects.fix: Add a "resolver" and "must clear by" field to every row and sort placeholders into three classes: (1) pre-submission blockers, EY-supplied (C-07 to C-13, C-19, C-25 to C-32, C-72); (2) pre-submission blockers, CI-supplied (C-03, and the missing LOE text); (3) inception-stage data requests (C-40, C-43). Class 3 must not appear as a placeholder in the PDFs - convert each into a stated, named assumption plus an inception-report data request, so the technical proposal reads as deliberate rather than incomplete.

defects.defect: C-08 and C-70 both state that the five-year window in Part 1 bullet 4 "conflicts" with the three-year window in criterion 2.2, and C-08 builds a risk rating on it. They do not conflict - they nest. "Relevant services undertaken in the past five (5) years" is a superset of "relevant services provided in the last three years"; a single dated list covering 2021-2026 satisfies both, with the 2023-2026 entries flagged. Calling a nested requirement a conflict inflates two risk ratings on false grounds and, worse, would generate a clarification question to CI that advertises a misreading of a simple instruction - on a bid where criterion 1.1 scores understanding of the ToR.
defects.fix: Replace "conflicts with" in both rows with "nests inside". Drop it from the clarification list. Build Annex B as one dated table covering 2021-2026 with a marked three-year sub-set, and reference the same annex from both Part 1 bullet 4 and the criterion 2.2 response. Re-rate C-08's risk on the real ground - that no EY assignment list exists yet - rather than on a phantom conflict.

defects.defect: C-34 tells the drafter that Activity One "is already partly done" and the matrix repeatedly leans on the head start (C-06, C-34, C-62) without guarding the commercial consequence. An evaluator scoring the 30-mark financial criterion on "reality to market value / value for money" who reads that a 31-benchmark scan and seven-archetype frame already exist will reasonably ask why the assignment still costs US$40,000. Presenting pre-existing work as delivered scope invites a price challenge on the criterion that carries nearly a third of the total, and also reads as presumptuous on a competitively tendered assignment.
defects.fix: Add a positioning instruction to C-34 and C-06: frame the prior scan as EY's own investment that buys CI more depth per dollar - 13 deep-dives rather than a shallower scan within the same envelope, and interviews started in week 1 rather than week 4 - not as work already delivered against CI's scope. Never state or imply that any part of Activity One is complete. Add a QA check that the phrases "already done", "already complete" and equivalents appear nowhere in either PDF.

defects.defect: C-16's risk field asserts "EY Business Consulting South Africa prices in ZAR, so conversion is unavoidable" as established fact. This is not in any input. It is a plausible inference from the engagement partner's location, but it is exactly the class of unverified firm-specific fact the integrity rule exists to catch, and it drives a whole FX-disclosure and rate-source workstream that may be unnecessary if EY SA holds an approved USD rate card for development-sector clients.
defects.fix: Recast as a question inside the existing C-19 placeholder: "[[TO CONFIRM: EY SA to confirm whether an approved USD rate card exists for development-sector/NGO clients, or whether rates are ZAR-based and require conversion; if conversion is needed, supply the rate, source and date to be disclosed]]". Make the FX-disclosure requirement in C-16 conditional on that answer rather than assumed.

defects.defect: C-03 files the Signed Offeror Representation of Transparency, Integrity, Social Responsibility as "Technical Proposal Annex D". The RFP lists it as a third, co-equal item in the completeness table alongside Technical Proposal and Cost Proposal, not as a component of either. Burying a separately named mandatory submission item inside another document's annex risks it being logged as not submitted by whoever checks completeness at CI's end - and C-03's own risk field says an absent form makes the whole proposal incomplete.
defects.fix: Submit the signed representation as its own PDF alongside the two proposal PDFs, and additionally annex a copy at Annex D. Update C-03's whereMet to "standalone signed PDF, with copy at Technical Proposal Annex D" and add it to the QA release checklist as a third file.

defects.defect: C-05 states EY's understanding of the problem as "15 prioritised emerging protected areas in Southern, Eastern and Western Africa" with no qualification, while C-71 separately notes the RFP is internally inconsistent on exactly this point. The RFP first says CI "has prioritized 15 emerging protected areas in Southern and Eastern Africa" and then, two sentences later, "These are spread across Southern, Eastern and Western Africa." Picking one reading silently in the row that feeds criterion 1.1 - the criterion that scores whether EY understood the ToR - means a 50 percent chance of appearing to have misread CI's own first formulation.
defects.fix: In C-05, instruct the drafter to mirror CI's wording rather than resolve it: "15 emerging protected areas prioritised by CI's Tourism Technical Assistance team, which the ToR describes as spanning Southern, Eastern and (at one point) Western Africa". Add the sub-region question to the clarification list and to the inception-report data request alongside C-40.

defects.defect: C-57 claims multi-segment stratification is the aim "where most cases score low" in EY's benchmark ratings. Counting the "Segments and appeal" column in Section 4 of the research draft gives 11 L, 13 M, 5 H and 2 unrated across the 31 benchmarks. Low is the largest single L-count of any column, and H-count of 5 is the lowest, so "weakest-evidenced aim" holds - but "most cases score low" does not, since M outnumbers L. A compliance matrix that overstates its own evidence base by a third invites correction from the team member who owns the ratings.
defects.fix: Change to "the least strongly evidenced aim in the current ratings - only five of 31 benchmarks rate H, the lowest H-count of any column - so it needs deliberate attention in the deep-dives rather than assumed coverage." Name the five H-rated cases if any are cited: World Heritage Journeys, SLH, Signature Experiences of Australia, National Trust and Brand USA.

defects.defect: C-74 recommends "a visible compliance cross-reference table in the technical proposal" as "cheap insurance", but does not say where it sits. Part 1 is capped at 5 pages and C-15's risk already rates compression severe. A cross-reference table mapping six evaluation criteria to their locations will consume a meaningful fraction of that cap if placed in the Part 1 body, so the insurance is not cheap - it is paid for out of the scarcest resource in the bid.
defects.fix: Specify placement in C-74: the cross-reference table goes on the technical proposal's contents page or in a dedicated annex, outside the Part 1 page count. Confirm in QA that the page count for Part 1 is measured on the narrative body only, excluding cover, contents and cross-reference table.

defects.defect: C-23 specifies the payment schedule's structure, percentages and the 10% inception cap, but says nothing about payment terms - days from CI's written acceptance to payment, or from invoice. With a maximum 10% (US$4,000 or less) payable at week 2 and the bulk of the research effort front-loaded into weeks 1 to 5, EY funds most of the engagement before the second milestone clears. The matrix flags no working-capital exposure and proposes no terms.
defects.fix: Extend C-23's evidenceNeeded to include a stated payment term (for example, net 30 days from CI's written acceptance of each deliverable) and add a line to the cost proposal's assumptions. Add an open item: "[[TO CONFIRM: EY SA finance to confirm acceptable payment terms and whether the working-capital profile implied by a 10% inception milestone at week 2 requires sign-off]]".

defects.defect: C-35's list of global platform cases omits EDEN (European Destinations of Excellence), which EY's own research draft describes as "the closest precedent for CI's core problem: visibility for emerging places" and whose 2019 evaluation the draft puts "on the Activity One reading list". The row lists seven commercial collections, three standards platforms and three revenue engines but leaves out the one benchmark the research names as the closest match to CI's actual problem statement. World Heritage Journeys and Alpine Pearls are likewise absent from the row while appearing elsewhere in the matrix.
defects.fix: Add EDEN to C-35's evidenceNeeded, with the note that the 2019 Commission evaluation explains why support was narrowed to a single winner - directly relevant to whether CI should spread thin support across 15 areas or concentrate it. Add World Heritage Journeys and Alpine Pearls to the same list so the row reflects the full place-marketer set rather than only the curator set.

strengths: Structural coverage of the ToR is complete and verified line by line. All nine model-elaboration headings from Section 2 map one-to-one to C-44 through C-52; all seven design aims map to C-53 through C-59; all eight key skills from Section 3 map to C-25 through C-32. No heading, aim or skill is duplicated, merged or dropped. This is the part most compliance matrices get wrong and it is right here.

Evaluation weights are transcribed accurately and reconcile: 1.1 = 5, 1.2 = 20, 2.1 = 5, 2.2 = 15, 2.4 = 10, 3.1 = 15, totalling the stated 70, with the financial 30 correctly carrying the full 'inclusive of any applicable tax, reimbursables and travel' wording.

Placeholder discipline against the integrity rule is strong and consistent. Every EY credential, client name, referee, CV, staff name, day rate, legal entity and tax position is placeheld with a named supplier and a specific description of what would satisfy it. No EY reference, rate or person is asserted anywhere in 74 rows. Michael Harris is the only named individual and he comes from the brief.

Every benchmark fact drawn into the matrix checks out against the research draft: ECST 164 areas to 91, Alpine Pearls about 24 villages to 18, LHW's paid Leaders Club ending in 2021, Relais & Chateaux members reporting EUR3.308bn in 2025, Harpers Ferry printing 24-28 million brochures a year for 400+ park units, the Event Book across Namibia's 86 conservancies, and the 31 benchmarks / seven archetypes / 13 deep-dives (8 Tier 1 plus 5 Tier 2) count.

No arithmetic to break. The matrix asserts no budget figure, no percentage split and no total, so there is no ceiling breach, no failed sum and no percentage set that misses 100. The 10% inception cap (C-23) and the US$40,000 ceiling (C-24) are stated as constraints to be tested at QA rather than pre-empted with invented numbers, which is the correct posture at this stage.

Several genuinely sharp readings that a weaker matrix would miss: that 'descriptions and Documentation' in criterion 3.1 makes CVs mandatory in practice despite Part 2's permissive 'may' (C-10, C-72); that 'proven ability to work with the private sector and secure investment' sets an outcome test rather than an advisory test (C-28); that a branding-agency-flavoured proposal would fail the explicit out-of-scope boundary and cost marks on criterion 1.1 (C-60); that the presentation count in the Deliverable 3 footnote is unbounded and unpriceable under a no-revision rule (C-66); and that the financial criterion's reference to travel and reimbursables sits in tension with the desk-based scope and must be answered rather than ignored (C-61, C-73).

Risk ratings are well calibrated overall. The High ratings sit almost exactly on the rows that cannot be drafted at all without EY input - C-07 to C-13, C-19, C-22, C-25, C-27, C-28, C-32, C-68, C-70, C-72 - and the Low ratings sit on the rows EY's existing benchmark scan already answers. The matrix correctly identifies criterion 1.2 at 20 marks as the highest-weighted and least-evidenced item, and names it the top bid-preparation priority.

defects.defect: The four options are not structured against the nine headings the RFP mandates. The RFP requires every brand-delivery support model to elaborate: services/offer; expected results; stakeholders; information and cash flows; funding needs and requirements over time; governance and management structures; potential funders and investors; case studies/inspiration/lessons; and pros and cons from the perspective of national government, park authorities, collaborative management partners, communities, visitors and private sector. The analysis uses a private schema (oneLine / offer / payer / governance / anchorBenchmarks / sustainabilityLogic / keyRisk) that covers only four of the nine cleanly. Entirely absent: EXPECTED RESULTS (named twice in the RFP - in the nine headings and again in Activity Two's recommendation bullet), STAKEHOLDERS as a discrete heading, INFORMATION FLOWS (only the Shared Studio mentions a data spine; the other three are silent), FUNDING NEEDS OVER TIME (no time-phased profile anywhere), and PROS AND CONS FROM THE SIX NAMED PERSPECTIVES - substituted by a single 'keyRisk' per model, which is EY's risk, not the six stakeholders' balance sheet. This is self-inflicted: EY's own research, Section 7, instructs that 'every deep-dive should follow the nine headings CI uses for model design, from the offer and expected results through cash flows, governance and funders to stakeholder pros and cons, so benchmark evidence drops straight into the options.' The analysis abandons its own method.
defects.fix: Rebuild each option on the nine RFP headings verbatim as the field names, in the RFP's order. Add the five missing fields per model. For pros and cons, use a 6-row table per model (national government / park authorities / collaborative management partners / communities / visitors / private sector) - 24 rows across four models. Where a stakeholder view cannot be evidenced from the benchmarks, placehold it as a question for the Activity Two stakeholder sessions rather than guessing.

defects.defect: The Co-Brand Hub keyRisk states 'Every place marketer rates L or M on self-funding.' This is false against EY's own Section 4 matrix: Africa's Eden Tourism, a place marketer, rates H on self-funding. It is also self-contradictory - the analysis's own revenueModules section calls Africa's Eden 'the only African cross-border identity in the scan that the private sector pays for,' which is precisely why it rates H. An evaluator holding both documents sees EY contradict itself, and it happens on a benchmark CI named by name in the RFP.
defects.fix: Rewrite as: 'Six of the seven place marketers rate L or M on self-funding; the single exception, Africa's Eden Tourism, rates H - and it is the one that charges its members. That is the design lesson, not a footnote: a place marketer funds itself only when the private sector pays to be in it.' This turns the error into the strongest argument for the option.

defects.defect: The Keystone Collection keyRisk states 'Every curator benchmark rates L on low-capacity fit.' False on EY's own Section 4 matrix: of the seven curator and distributor benchmarks, Experience Mekong Collection rates H on low-capacity fit and Signature Experiences of Australia rates M. Only five of seven rate L. The claim is checkable in one glance at the matrix EY is handing CI as its scoring frame.
defects.fix: Correct to 'Five of the seven curator benchmarks rate L on low-capacity fit,' and name the two exceptions - they are the evidence that a curator CAN serve low-capacity members, which materially strengthens the option rather than weakening it.

defects.defect: The Keystone Collection sustainabilityLogic asserts 'the collection can reach break-even at 20 to 30 members instead of the several hundred an independent consortium needs.' Neither figure appears anywhere in the 31-benchmark research; there is no cost or fee data in the scan from which either could be derived. It is a fabricated quantitative claim about the economics of the model EY is steering CI toward - and it is contradicted two sentences later in the same option's keyRisk, which states that member fee structures for LHW, SLH, Beyond Green and National Geographic 'are all unpublished, which means the economics of CI's preferred complex version are currently unknown.' You cannot state a break-even range and state the economics are unknown in the same option.
defects.fix: Delete the break-even figures. Replace with: 'Hosting rather than building removes the largest fixed cost, so the break-even membership should be materially lower than the several hundred members the long-established independent consortia carry. The actual figure is unknown: no collection in the scan publishes its fee structure. [[TO CONFIRM: indicative membership fee and commission terms for a hosted sustainability sub-collection - to be sought from Preferred Hotel Group and SLH during the Activity One deep-dives; if not obtained, the model will be costed on a stated range with the assumption declared]]'

defects.defect: Experience Mekong Collection is dropped entirely from all four options, despite being one of the 31 benchmarks and the only curator in the scan that rates H on low-capacity fit. It is the Mekong Tourism Coordinating Office curating 350+ small responsible businesses across six countries against three tests (community impact, authentic local experience, viable business model), giving members a certified badge, a feature page, a free booth at the Mekong Tourism Forum and discounted marketing services. That is a low-cost cross-border curation brand for exactly the kind of thin, emerging, low-capacity supply CI is describing - and the direct answer to the objection the analysis itself raises against the Keystone Collection. Its L on self-funding is the honest counterweight and should be shown too.
defects.fix: Add Experience Mekong Collection to the Keystone Collection anchorBenchmarks with its scale (350+ businesses, six countries, est. 2017) and its three admission tests, framed as the low-capacity entry tier beneath the commercial hosting arrangement - and state its L self-funding rating openly as the reason it is a tier rather than the whole model.

defects.defect: The evaluation frame covers only 8 of the 11 tests the RFP names. Of CI's seven design aims it scores six - it drops the seventh entirely ('Reference and compare the approaches to existing efforts in the market to ensure the model is tailored to fill gaps rather than duplicate efforts') and narrows the sixth from 'promote mechanisms that support multi-stakeholder brand management, including reconciling alignment with national destination brands' down to 'fit with national destination brands,' losing the multi-stakeholder brand management half. Of Activity Two's four stated conditions ('effective cross-jurisdiction, in unstable funding environments, across multiple stakeholders, and for protected areas with wide ranging capacity') it scores two, dropping 'unstable funding environments' and 'across multiple stakeholders.' Dropping unstable funding environments is the serious one: every option in the set leans on donor, public or association money, and that is the exact resilience test CI asked for. The substance of the non-duplication aim IS argued well in all four option narratives; it simply is not in the instrument EY is offering CI as the scoring frame, which is where CI will check for it.
defects.fix: Extend the frame to eleven criteria: add 'non-duplication / fills a gap in the existing market', 'resilience in unstable funding environments', and 'multi-stakeholder brand management' as scored columns, and rename 'national brand fit' to 'multi-stakeholder brand management and national destination brand alignment'. State explicitly that the frame maps one-to-one onto CI's seven design aims plus Activity Two's four conditions, plus African evidence as EY's own addition.

defects.defect: RFP 5.2 requires that for each concept EY provide 'scope, offer, approach, governance, management, budget and funding sources'; that 'Pre-requisites will also be important to consider'; and (Purpose of Assessment) 'a critical evaluation and feasibility of each'. The analysis has no indicative budget for any of the four models, no management structure distinct from governance, no pre-requisites, and no feasibility assessment. 'sustainabilityLogic' answers how a model pays for itself once running; it does not answer what it costs to stand up, what must be true first, or whether it is feasible at all.
defects.fix: Add three fields per model: an indicative set-up and annual running cost band with the basis stated; 'pre-requisites' (what must exist before the model can start - e.g. for the Keystone Mark, a published criteria manual and at least one willing national operator per country; for the Co-Brand Hub, a signed commitment from at least two national tourism boards); and a short feasibility verdict against those pre-requisites. Where a cost cannot be evidenced from the scan, use a placeholder naming the deep-dive that will produce it.

defects.defect: Part 1 of the technical proposal is capped at a maximum of 5 pages excluding annexes. This analysis, rendered at anything close to its current depth, is several times that on its own - four models with seven or more fields each, five to six anchor benchmarks per model, seven revenue modules and an evaluation frame. The analysis carries no signal about what lands inside the 5 pages and what goes to an annex, so as it stands it is a page-cap breach waiting to happen.
defects.fix: Decide the split now and record it: inside Part 1, the framing note compressed to three or four sentences, the four model one-liners, and the eleven-criterion evaluation frame as a single table. Everything else - full model elaborations against the nine headings, anchor benchmarks, revenue modules - goes to a clearly titled annex, cross-referenced from Part 1. Confirm CI accepts annexes of this kind; if the RFP is silent beyond 'excluding annexes', keep the annex tight and self-evidently supporting rather than a second proposal.

defects.defect: The framing note commits EY to outcomes that depend on third parties who have not agreed to anything: the deep-dives 'will price the shared studio, establish whether a certification mark can fund itself, ask Preferred Hotel Group and SLH what hosting a Keystone collection would actually cost, and put the hard outcome questions to the Boundless Southern Africa and Africa's Eden secretariats.' EY's own research says the opposite about access: none of these organisations publishes cost or outcome data, member fee structures for LHW, Relais & Chateaux, SLH, Preferred, National Geographic and The Long Run are all unpublished, and the whole reason interviews are prioritised is that the data is not otherwise obtainable. Preferred Hotel Group and SLH have no commercial reason to disclose hosting terms to a bidder on someone else's RFP. Promising this flatly in a bid is a promise EY may not be able to keep, and CI will hold the final report to it.
defects.fix: Reframe as intent plus fallback: 'We will approach Preferred Hotel Group and SLH on hosting terms and the Boundless and Africa's Eden secretariats on outcomes. Where an organisation declines or does not respond within the window, we will say so in the report and model the gap on a stated, sourced range rather than leave it blank - and we will name in the inception report which approaches are underway.' Add [[TO CONFIRM: whether CI or the Keystone Partnership can open doors to the Boundless Southern Africa and Africa's Eden secretariats and to Preferred Hotel Group - supplied by CI's Tourism Technical Assistance team at inception]].

defects.defect: 'The only archetype in the scan that consistently rates high on self-funding' overstates the curator and distributor row. Five of seven rate H (LHW, Relais & Chateaux, SLH, Beyond Green, National Geographic); Signature Experiences of Australia rates M and Experience Mekong Collection rates L. 'Consistently' will be checked against the matrix on the facing page.
defects.fix: Change to 'The archetype with the strongest self-funding record in the scan: five of its seven benchmarks rate H, more than any other group.' The claim survives scrutiny and loses nothing.

defects.defect: The Co-Brand Hub cites Visit Rwanda's Arsenal sleeve deal in the present tense - 'about GBP 10m a year to Arsenal and more than GBP 80m over eight years'. The research states the Arsenal deal 'ended with the 2025/26 season', which is now past. Presenting a concluded sponsorship as live in a September 2026 bid is the kind of slip an evaluator with a football-following colleague notices immediately.
defects.fix: Rewrite as 'about GBP 10m a year to Arsenal and more than GBP 80m over eight years, concluded with the 2025/26 season, with PSG, Bayern Munich and Atletico Madrid deals continuing.' The point about a park brand sitting beneath the national brand is unaffected and better evidenced by the deals still running.

defects.defect: The Brand USA revenue module is internally inconsistent on the match cap. It states the match is 'capped at US$100m a year and up to US$200m in total' as a present-tense fact, then states in the same paragraph that '2025 legislation cut the match cap to US$20m'. Both cannot be current. The operative cap today is US$20m - an 80% cut that is itself the most useful part of the lesson for CI.
defects.fix: Rewrite as 'unlocked a 1:1 match capped at US$100m a year and US$200m in total, until 2025 legislation cut the annual cap to US$20m.' Then draw the lesson explicitly: a match facility can be legislated away, so a Keystone match should be secured contractually with its funder rather than assumed.

defects.defect: The Keystone Collection describes National Geographic Unique Lodges as 'sold through Virtuoso advisers'. The research says something narrower: itineraries link to National Geographic Private Expeditions, which are sold through Virtuoso advisers. The lodge collection itself is not stated to be distributed by Virtuoso.
defects.fix: Correct to 'with linked National Geographic Private Expeditions itineraries sold through Virtuoso advisers' - which still makes the borrowed-distribution point accurately.

defects.defect: The research carries an explicit standing caveat - 'All figures are as published by the sources below, accessed September 2026. They have not yet been verified with the organisations concerned.' The analysis drops it and states all 31 benchmarks' figures flatly. Most exposed is the assertion that Boundless Southern Africa has 'no published measure of recognition, trade adoption or bookings in 18 years'. The research supports 'we found no published measures of recognition or bookings' - an absence of evidence from a desk scan - not the stronger claim that none exists. CI named Boundless in the RFP; its secretariat sits inside the SADC Tourism Programme and EY intends to interview it. Asserting an 18-year void as fact, unverified, about an organisation in CI's own network is a needless risk, and 'trade adoption' is EY's addition to the list.
defects.fix: Carry the caveat into the proposal once, up front: 'Figures are as published by each source, accessed September 2026, and not yet verified with the organisations concerned; verification is part of Activity One.' Soften the Boundless claim to 'our desk scan found activity reporting but no published measures of recognition or bookings; establishing whether such measures exist internally is the first question of the deep-dive.'

defects.defect: The research carries an explicit disambiguation warning on Africa's Eden - 'Mind the name: a separate Netherlands-based operator called Africa's Eden runs conservation tourism in Gabon, the Central African Republic and Sao Tome and Principe.' The analysis drops it and references 'Africa's Eden' and 'the Africa's Eden model' without qualification. CI named Africa's Eden in the RFP, so CI knows which one it means; conflating them, or appearing to, damages the one place where EY most needs to look precise.
defects.fix: On first mention write 'Africa's Eden Tourism, the Botswana-domiciled regional membership association (distinct from the Netherlands-based Africa's Eden operator working in Gabon, CAR and Sao Tome and Principe)' and use the full name thereafter. It costs one line and demonstrates exactly the familiarity criterion 2.4 scores.

defects.defect: There is no West or Central African content anywhere in the analysis. Every African benchmark and every geography named sits in Southern or Eastern Africa - Namibia, Kenya, Botswana, Zambia, Zimbabwe, Tanzania, South Africa, Eswatini, Mozambique, Madagascar, Rwanda, Morocco. The RFP states the 15 prioritised areas 'are spread across Southern, Eastern and Western Africa', and EY's own research picked this up ('CI's 15 areas span Southern, Eastern and Western Africa'). Criterion 2.4, Geographical Reach and Familiarity, carries 10 of the 70 technical points, and the models as drafted lean hard on Southern and Eastern African conservancy-association infrastructure (NRT, NACSO, MMWCA) that has no West African equivalent in the scan.
defects.fix: Add a short, honest paragraph: name the asymmetry, note that the shared-service option's reliance on existing associations is a Southern and Eastern African strength that does not travel west, and state that West and Central African institutional mapping - including francophone delivery, and whether Africa's Eden's Gabon/CAR/Sao Tome work offers a route - is a named Activity One task once CI supplies the list of 15. Tie it to the existing [[TO CONFIRM]] on the 15 areas.

defects.defect: Scope realism against the ceiling. Four models, each properly elaborated against the nine RFP headings including six stakeholder perspectives, is 24 stakeholder assessments plus 36 other populated fields, on top of eight case-study deep-dives and five light-touch checks - inside US$40,000, 12 weeks, desk-based. EY's own research states the constraint plainly: 'The budget sets the depth. At US$40,000 over 12 weeks, fully desk-based, eight case studies (two of them clustered) and five light-touch checks is the most the programme can carry.' The fourth model is a genuine differentiator, but offering it without showing how it fits the envelope invites the evaluator scoring criterion B (30 points for reality to market value) to conclude EY has under-priced or will under-deliver.
defects.fix: Show the load explicitly. State that all four options are developed to the nine headings at concept depth, that the evidence base is shared across them (the 31-benchmark scan is already sunk cost, borne by EY), and that depth is concentrated on the two or three that survive the week-5 screen - with CI choosing which at the deliverable 2 review. That makes four options look efficient rather than expensive.

defects.defect: The framing note pre-announces the conclusion: 'We expect at least one option to be discarded and the recommended model to be a hybrid.' Activity Two requires EY to 'make justified recommendations for selection of the preferred model'. If the recommendation is a hybrid, CI ends up with a preferred model that sits outside the four that were actually evaluated against the frame - and an evaluator can read the sentence as EY having decided the answer before Activity One has started, which cuts directly against the framing note's own argument.
defects.fix: Add one sentence: 'If the recommendation is a hybrid, it will itself be elaborated against all nine headings and scored on the same frame as the standalone options, so CI never has to choose a model that has not been evaluated.' Consider softening 'we expect' to 'the benchmark evidence points toward' - it keeps the honesty without pre-judging.

defects.defect: The Shared Studio is labelled 'CI's stated simple version, the grant-funded technical assistance retainer', but it is not CI's version. CI describes 'a grant-funded technical assistance coaching service (a firm on retention) that parks can draw down on'. The analysis removes the firm-on-retention element and substitutes hosting inside an existing conservancy association, with 'No new legal entity in phase one. The studio is hosted inside an existing association or as a CI-managed facility.' The reasoning is good and the non-duplication logic is one of the strongest passages in the analysis - but it is stated as settled when EY's own deep-dive list still carries 'Whether they would host or join a CI facility' as an open question for NRT, NACSO and MMWCA. Claiming identity with CI's concept while quietly changing it is the kind of thing that costs points on criterion 1.1, understanding of the ToR.
defects.fix: Name the deviation and own it: 'CI's simple version is a firm on retention. We think the retainer should be delivered through the conservancy associations that already serve these areas rather than as a standalone consultancy line, because the aggregation layer exists and CI's own terms ask the model to fill gaps rather than duplicate. Whether those associations would host such a facility is an open question and the first thing the NRT, NACSO and MMWCA deep-dives must answer.' Add a placeholder for association willingness.

strengths: The integrity rule is honoured cleanly. Across the whole analysis there is not one invented EY credential, client name, staff name, CV detail, rate or reference. The single placeholder present is correctly formed and genuinely specific about both what is needed and who supplies it (CI's list of the 15 prioritised areas and any weighting across CI's design aims, from CI's Tourism Technical Assistance team at inception). This is the most serious failure mode available and the analysis does not commit it.

Benchmark accuracy is high. I checked roughly thirty discrete data points against the research draft - Blue Flag's 4,302 beaches / 736 marinas / 158 boats in 52 countries and 33 beach criteria; Geoparks' 229 in 48 countries at May 2026 and the green/yellow/red four-year cycle; ECST's 164-areas-in-20-countries to 91-in-13 contraction with 1,500+ business partners and 41 tour operators; Slovenia Green's 200+ members and 59 destinations, GoodPlace, ETIS and GSTC, and the Karst and Brkini municipal merger; Fair Trade Tourism's 188 businesses in eight countries with the correct split between own certification and mutual recognition, and the EUR 3,000 package cost; NACSO's 86 conservancies, 166,000 km2, 245,000 people, 42 joint-venture lodges and N$75m at 64%; MMWCA's 24 conservancies, 178,700 ha, 16,500 landowners, 50 tourism partners and the US$5m Maasai Mara Rescue Fund; Harpers Ferry's 100+ staff, 400+ units and 24-28 million brochures; National Trust's GBP 766.2m, GBP 309.4m, 2.61m memberships, 5.35m people, 25.9m visits, 83.3% retention, 403,000 joiners and the GBP 48 tier at +39%; SANParks' five agencies and R835 / R1,375 / R1,680 / R3,780; Relais & Chateaux's 580 in 65 countries and EUR 3.308bn with applications up 14% to 615; Beyond Green's 24 founding members in 15 countries with the African lodges named correctly; National Geographic's 24 charter lodges with the five African properties named correctly. Three misstatements in thirty is a good hit rate for a document of this density.

The framing note is the best-written passage and does real work. Declaring starting hypotheses openly, committing to at least one being discarded, and saying 'a bidder with no starting position has nothing for CI to argue with' pre-empts the standard objection to a bidder who arrives with answers. It converts EY's head start from a liability into the differentiator it actually is, and it speaks directly to criterion 1.1.

Each option carries a keyRisk that genuinely undercuts it, drawn from EY's own evidence rather than manufactured for balance - the shared service's permanent grant dependency, the mark's credibility-without-demand problem, the place marketer's worst-in-scan durability record, the collection's inability to reach the very areas CI cares about. Bidders almost never do this and evaluators notice when someone does.

Reusing the Section 4 matrix as the Activity Two scoring frame is a real methodological move, not a claim. It means Activity One evidence carries through to Activity Two by construction rather than by assertion, and it is exactly what criterion 2.1 (methodology and delivery in the timelines) is looking for. Saying 'the weighting is CI's to set, not ours' and 'the scoring is shown so CI can dispute it' is the right posture.

The four options span CI's stated spectrum properly and anchor both poles CI named itself - the grant-funded technical assistance retainer at one end, the Leading Hotels of the World analogue at the other - while adding a fourth that answers the requirement to reconcile with national destination brands. Four exceeds the 'at least three' minimum without padding.

The 'host before build' sequencing for the Keystone Collection is the single strongest design idea in the set: it answers CI's complex version in the order that de-risks it, and the explicit step-in and exit clause shows commercial thinking that most conservation bidders will not bring.

The revenue modules map onto CI's named streams - wild cards via the SANParks Wild Card, tiered memberships via the National Trust, merchandise via Certified Wildlife Friendly and Fair Trade Tourism - with African proof points attached rather than generic assertions, and with the counter-evidence included (memberships slipping 0.4%, LHW abandoning its paid tier). The Rewilding Europe module even names the commodification-of-nature critique as a stakeholder risk to design against, which is sourced and shows unusual self-awareness.
